C01.why: Anomaly horror with friends screaming at a faceless guest or a missed anomaly turning into a chase is a proven creator format (Sell Fries!, Exit 8), and a creepy motel at night makes a clear thumbnail. The weak point is that spotting a subtle anomaly needs context, so a 15-second clip only works when it escalates.
C01.fix: Make every missed anomaly end in a loud, readable payoff (a chase or jumpscare from the CCTV angle) and add a one-tap 'night recap' reel of the best scares, so each night produces a clip that makes sense with no context.

C02.why: Keep Talking went viral on the yelling, and emote-only communication removes most of that comedy. The confetti-blast ragdoll is a funny fail, but a silent 15-second clip of icon pings and a grey device is hard to follow.
C02.fix: Turn on optional proximity voice for age-verified lobbies and make the failure blast huge and cartoonish (players launched out of windows), so the fail reads instantly and becomes the clip.

C03.why: Six friends on a wobbly raft spinning into a waterfall reads instantly with no context, and the shared blame of 'who hit the left thruster?!' is natural friend-group chaos. Bathtub and shopping-cart vehicles give thumbnails that show exactly what you play.
C03.fix: Add slow-motion 'wipeout cam' replays and a post-race 'Who Sank Us' stat card showing each player's thruster input, so blame moments are built to be shared.

C04.why: The 'it was FAKE all along' reveal and the secret-forger mode give some betrayal payoff. But careful inspection with magnifiers and UV is slow to watch, and the thumbnail is a shop counter.
C04.fix: Add dramatic reveal moments (a fake vase shatters to show a 'MADE IN 2026' sticker, a fake fossil turns out to be chicken bones) and a forger unmasking cutscene, so each deal ends in a visual punchline.

C05.why: The premise is instantly relatable and works as a thumbnail with no explanation (a trashed house, Mom at the door). It stacks physics chaos, panic, hiding in plain sight, pushing the dog over the stain and snitch betrayals into short moments a 15-second clip shows clearly. Creators can roleplay the Parent.
C05.fix: Add a post-round 'Mom's Report Card' slideshow of the most absurd hiding spots and snitch moments, and a Parent 'gasp' reaction cam, giving a ready-made shareable punchline each round.

C06.why: This is mostly incremental grinding and conveyor building, which creators rarely clip. The giant haystack is a recognisable image, and a server-wide needle find is a small moment, not a reaction.
C06.fix: Make needle finds a server-wide spectacle (the pile erupts, a golden beam shoots up, a race to the spot) and add hazards inside the hay (rats, a collapsing pile burying machines) to create unexpected moments.

C07.why: A rope-linked group falling together is a proven YouTube format (PEAK, Chained Together), and it produces blame and laughter that read in seconds. Roblox already has many chained-together obbies, and snap-to-ledge climbing reduces the messy physics that make the best fails.
C07.fix: Keep the physics loose and dramatic (pendulum swings, one friend catching three falling teammates) and make the summit photo capture the whole run, including the worst fall, so there is a distinctive shareable image.

C08.why: Making footage the score is a built-in sharing loop (Content Warning grew this way), and horror-comedy grabs and bait/cameraman antics suit creators well. The risk is that server-side tags give a weak in-lobby montage rather than footage players can share.
C08.fix: Render the theatre montage as a real replay that captures cleanly with Roblox capture, ending on a fake 'views/comments' screen, so every run ends with a clip ready to post.

C09.why: Spell combos like a firenado look great, and misdrawn runes can backfire in funny ways. But wave defence is a familiar view that holds little surprise in 15 seconds, and drawing on a phone screen doesn't show up well on camera.
C09.fix: Add a misfire table where badly drawn runes produce absurd results (chickens instead of lightning, shrinking a teammate) and team ultimate combos with screen-filling visuals, so fails and combos both make clips.

C10.why: Weird mutation hatches ('my critter has three heads and a fish tail') can be shareable, but tactical auto-battles on a small board make poor clips and need context.
C10.fix: Make hatch reveals a dramatic gacha-style animation with absurd, visually loud mutations, and let players show family trees and critters in a shared lobby.

C11.why: Liminal pools and malls are a recognisable viral look, and noise-hunting entity chases while carrying loot give strong scream-and-run clips (R.E.P.O.-style). It sits in a crowded liminal space and lacks a signature funny mechanic, so it reads as one more backrooms game.
C11.fix: Add one signature mechanic that makes a hook, such as artifacts that make silly noises when carried, or a loud ragdoll stumble when caught, so clips mix comedy with horror.

C12.why: A burning plane crash-landing on a runway makes a dramatic, readable 15-second clip, and the panic of a crew that can't communicate is funny. The info-split coordination is mostly invisible on camera.
C12.fix: Make crashes and belly-landings spectacular and survivable (passengers flying out, landing in the sea), and add a cockpit cam replay with the outcome rating, so every landing ends as a clip.

C13.why: Betrayal among 50 players is good drama, and timelapse maps can go viral. But the 2D map view is abstract and needs narration, which suits long-form commentary more than shorts.
C13.fix: Auto-generate an end-of-match territory timelapse with betrayal markers ('X backstabbed Y') that players can share, to give the betrayal story a visual punchline.

C14.why: Carrying a wedding cake through a revolving door or dropping a fish tank on the stairs gives instantly readable physics fails, and Totally Reliable Delivery Service showed that creators like this. Driving and loading between deliveries slows the pace.
C14.fix: Make destruction loud and messy (a cake splatting on the customer, fish flopping everywhere, the value meter crashing to $0 with a sad trombone) and keep drives short, so a fail happens in nearly every 15 seconds.

C15.why: Auto-battlers are mostly menu drafting and watching boards, with little surprise and no shared friend moment, so clips need context and don't travel.
C15.fix: Add physical toy-box knockouts where eliminated players' toys are dramatically smashed or launched off the table, plus a toy-chaos arena finale with big visuals.

C16.why: Chaotic pets (a cat knocking things off shelves, a dog eating a sock) are naturally funny and relatable, but a cozy chore loop produces few surprising peaks.
C16.fix: Add escalating absurd pet events (a goat on the roof, a parrot that snitches to the owner) and an owner-returns reveal where the house state is judged dramatically.

C17.why: A tower collapse is satisfying and readable in 15 seconds, and blaming the teammate who placed the last piece is good friend drama. But the format is familiar, and placing pieces is slow to watch.
C17.fix: Make collapses huge and dramatic (players standing on the tower ragdoll down, slow-motion fall cam), and add sabotage in versus mode for betrayal moments.

C18.why: A weekly giant-monster battle between servers could be a creator event, and voting on mutations gives weird monsters. But most of the week is gathering and training, which nobody shares.
C18.fix: Make the weekly battle a live spectator event with huge visuals and give each monster a goofy shareable profile card showing its voted mutations, so there is something to post all week.

C19.why: Freezing mid-prank as the flashlight sweeps past (drawing a moustache on a portrait, a dinosaur skeleton creeping behind the guard) is funny, tense and clear with no context, and the format fits creators well. The hide-in-plain-sight space is crowded, which dulls distinctiveness a little.
C19.fix: Add a 'caught on camera' security-footage replay at round end showing every prank the guard missed, to give a built-in shareable reveal.

C20.why: Competitive sports produce occasional highlight plays, but tap-to-aim removes flashy skill expression, and Volleyball Legends already owns volleyball clips with anime-style spikes.
C20.fix: Add exaggerated special spikes and physics chaos (ball knocking players over, net-cord moments) to give a distinctive visual identity beyond plain volleyball.

overall_notes: Clip potential clusters around physical chaos with shared blame (C03, C05, C07, C14), asymmetric deception (C05, C19) and co-op horror (C01, C08, C11). Grinding, menu or strategy concepts (C06, C10, C13, C15, C20) score low because a 15-second clip needs narration. Most of the top concepts can add a built-in end-of-round replay or reveal (report card, security footage, ghost montage, wipeout cam); this is the cheapest way to raise sharing. Every top concept has an honest thumbnail of the actual gameplay, so bait risk is low. Emote-only communication reduces the yelling comedy behind most co-op viral clips, which hurts C02 and C12 most.
